content: The pelvis, also referred to as the pelvic girdle, is a bony structure located at the base of the spine, specifically at its caudal end. It is a component of the appendicular skeleton. Each hip bone, or os coxae, is composed of three distinct bones: the ilium, the ischium, and the pubis. The ilium is the largest and uppermost portion of the hip bone. The ischium forms the posterior-inferior (back-lower) section, while the pubis constitutes the anterior (front) part of the hip bone. The two hip bones are connected anteriorly at the symphysis pubis and posteriorly to the sacrum. The pelvis also includes the socket portion of the hip joint, which accommodates the femoral head of each leg in bipeds or the hind legs in quadrupeds. Functionally, the pelvis forms the girdle for the lower limbs (or hind limbs in quadrupeds). Gender Differences in Pelvic Anatomy: The infrapubic angle is greater than 90 degrees in females, whereas it is less than 90 degrees in males. The pelvic inlet in males has a heart-shaped configuration, while in females, it is more rounded or oval in shape. The greater sciatic notch is narrower in males compared to females. The acetabulum in males is oriented more laterally, whereas in females, it faces more anteriorly. The sacrum in females is more triangular in shape. Types of Pelvis: 1. Gynaecoid Pelvis: This is the typical female pelvis. It is characterized by a rounded shape with an enlarged transverse diameter. 2. Android Pelvis: This is the typical male pelvis. It has a heart-shaped configuration. 3. Anthropoid Pelvis: This type of pelvis has a longer anterior-to-posterior diameter. 4. Platypelloid Pelvis: This type of pelvis is distinguished by a longer transverse diameter.
